# Sirach Chapter 38 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Vaticanus, Sirach 38 | **Agents Consulted:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA

---

## Council Notes

Chapter 38 is in two distinct parts. Part I (vv. 1–23) concerns medicine, illness, and mourning. The famous physician passage (vv. 1–15) is the most significant pro-medical text in ancient Jewish literature; it was cited throughout Christian history to justify medicine as a God-given discipline. Key points: (1) the physician is God's creation (v. 1); (2) medicines come from the earth as God's gift (v. 4); (3) prayer and medical treatment work together — neither replaces the other (vv. 9–14); (4) verse 15 is deliberately sharp: "whoever sins against his Maker, let him fall into the care of a physician" — probably ironic, suggesting the sinner needs earthly healing since spiritual healing has been forfeited.

Part II (vv. 24–34) opens the scribe-versus-laborer comparison. Ben Sira genuinely respects craftsmen (vv. 31–34: "they hold the world together") but argues the scribal life is the only path to wisdom because it requires leisure for study.

---

**38:1** Honor the physician with the honor due him, according to your need for him, for the Lord created him;

**38:2** for healing comes from the Most High, and he receives gifts from the king.

**38:3** The skill of the physician lifts up his head, and he is admired in the presence of great men.

**38:4** The Lord created medicines from the earth, and a sensible person will not refuse them.

**38:5** Was not water made sweet with a piece of wood, so that his power might become known to all?

**38:6** And he gave skill to human beings so that he might be glorified in his wondrous works.

**38:7** By them the physician takes away pain and heals, and the pharmacist compounds his remedies.

**38:8** There is no end to his works, and from him health spreads over all the earth.

**38:9** My child, when you are ill, do not neglect yourself, but pray to the Lord, and he will heal you.

**38:10** Turn aside from wrongdoing and make your hands do right, and cleanse your heart from all iniquity.

**38:11** Offer a sweet-smelling sacrifice and a memorial of fine flour, and pour oil upon your offering, as one who is not yet dead.

**38:12** Then give the physician his proper place, for the Lord created him as well; do not let him leave you, for there is need of him.

**38:13** There are times when recovery lies in the hands of physicians,

**38:14** for they too will pray to the Lord that he grant them success in diagnosis and healing — for the sake of the patient's life.

**38:15** Whoever sins before his Maker, let him fall into the care of a physician.

**38:16** My child, shed tears over the dead, and begin the lamentation as one who is suffering greatly; wrap the body as is fitting, and do not neglect the burial.

**38:17** Let your weeping be bitter and your wailing fervent; observe the mourning befitting the person, for one day or two, to avoid censure; then be comforted for your grief.

**38:18** For grief may result in death, and a grief-laden heart drains away strength.

**38:19** Sorrow abides when calamity comes, and the life of the poor weighs down the heart.

**38:20** Do not give your heart to grief; drive it away, and remember your own end.

**38:21** Do not forget — there is no returning; you cannot help him, and you can only harm yourself.

**38:22** "Remember my judgment, for yours will be the same: yesterday mine and today yours."

**38:23** When the dead is at rest, let his memory also rest; be comforted for him once his spirit has departed.

**38:24** The wisdom of the scribe depends on the opportunity of leisure; only the one who has little business may become wise.

**38:25** How can one who holds the goad become wise — who takes pride in wielding the goad, who drives oxen and is absorbed in their work, and whose talk is all about cattle?

**38:26** He sets his heart on making a straight furrow and stays anxious about fodder for the heifers.

**38:27** So too is every craftsman and master craftsman who works by night as well as by day; those who engrave seal designs, intent on producing a faithful likeness, who set their hearts on finishing the work.

**38:28** So too is the smith sitting at his forge, intent on his ironwork; the breath of fire scorches his flesh, and he contends with the heat of the furnace; the noise of the hammer deafens him; his eyes are fixed on the pattern of the object; he sets his heart on completing his work, and he stays up to give it a polished finish.

**38:29** So too is the potter, sitting at his work and turning the wheel with his feet; he is in constant anxiety over his work, and each piece is produced with care.

**38:30** He shapes the clay with his arm and treads it soft with his feet; he sets his heart on finishing the glazing, and stays up to clean the kiln.

**38:31** All of these trust in their hands, and each is skilled in his own craft.

**38:32** Without them a city cannot be built, and men can neither sojourn nor dwell there.

**38:33** Yet they are not sought for the council of the people, nor do they attain prominence in the public assembly. They do not sit in the judge's seat, nor do they understand the decisions of the covenant; they cannot expound instruction or judgment, and they are not found among those who use proverbs.

**38:34** But they sustain the fabric of this world, and their prayer is in the practice of their craft.
